query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloys, mechanical wear at elevated temperature disrupts protective, passivating layers and exposes heterogeneous phase boundaries (e.g., between ductile matrix and harder intermetallic or secondary phases). This exposure creates galvanically active micro‐regions that accelerate localized corrosion. The resulting corrosion damage, in turn, weakens the microstructure, further exacerbating the wear damage in a synergistic feedback loop.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a well‐developed, interpenetrating microstructure (e.g., a primary solid solution phase combined with secondary, intermetallic or Laves phases) that initially possesses a protective, continuous surface oxide/passive layer at room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to simultaneous mechanical wear (scratching/abrasion under controlled load) and a corrosive environment at an elevated temperature (conditions known to accelerate diffusion and chemical reactions) versus isolated exposures to wear or corrosion.
generation.conditions: Testing should occur at an elevated temperature (e.g., >900 °C but below melting temperature) in a corrosive medium representative of industrial acid or oxidative environments, with a controlled mechanical wear load that produces moderate surface damage without full removal of the entire sample.
generation.structural_mediator: Disruption of the continuous passive oxide layer and exposure of heterogeneous phase boundaries, which act as local sites for enhanced galvanic corrosion.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear degrades the integrity of the passive film, exposing phase boundaries where electrochemical potential differences between phases yield localized corrosion. The elevated temperature accelerates ionic transport and reaction kinetics, intensifying the corrosion rate. This corrosion then undermines the alloy’s microstructural cohesion, increasing wear susceptibility in a mutually reinforcing cycle.
generation.predicted_outcome: The total degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion will be significantly higher than the sum of degradation observed in isolated wear-only and corrosion-only tests. Specifically, both the wear rate and corrosion rate will individually increase relative to the baseline—indicating synergistic coupling where the removal of protective layers by wear leads to accelerated corrosion, and corrosion-induced material weakening further increases wear.
generation.baseline: A matched set of tests on similar specimens subjected solely to mechanical wear and solely to corrosion under identical temperature and environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under conditions where temperature is sufficiently high to promote rapid diffusion and reaction kinetics but not so high as to induce melting or entirely change the phase stability. Additionally, the alloy must exhibit a multiphase eutectic microstructure with distinct phase boundaries capable of supporting galvanic interactions.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the synergistic effect and its sensitivity to microstructural scale and phase distribution is uncertain; variations in the degree of phase coupling, oxide film stability, and mechanical load intensity may alter the observed acceleration in degradation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of eutectic high-entropy alloy specimens with similar initial microstructure. Divide them into three groups: (1) subject one group to controlled mechanical wear only, (2) subject another group to controlled corrosion only (using the same corrosive medium and elevated temperature), and (3) subject a third group to simultaneous wear and corrosion under identical temperature and environmental conditions. Use identical testing durations and workloads across groups.
measurements: Quantitative mass loss for overall degradation.
Surface profilometry and microscopy (SEM/EDS) to characterize wear track morphology and corrosion pit formation.
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., potentiostatic or potentiodynamic tests) to assess local corrosion rates at exposed phase boundaries.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the degradation (mass loss, surface damage, and electrochemical corrosion rate) measured in the simultaneous wear and corrosion test is not significantly greater than the sum (or additive effects) of those measured in the wear-only and corrosion-only tests, then the hypothesis that there is a synergistic, coupled enhancement of degradation via disruption of protective layers and localized corrosion is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm
